1. The animation shows a grid of historical start months, from January 1991 to July 2016. Each month is a tile. A lit tile means someone who bought that month was ahead of a renter after ten years. A dark tile means the renter was ahead. The label says the data comes from FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac rates. It is marked "illustrative", "US only" and "history, not a forecast".

2. Tiles light up over time. In frames 1 to 3, a narrow band lights up, and the caption says "72 start months in a row: 6 of 72". In frames 4 and 5, nearly the whole grid is lit, and the caption says "15 years: every one (100%)". A note says "the street ends where the data ends". The last start months are cut off because ten years of follow-up data don't exist for them. In frame 6, the grid goes dark and asks "Is her rent money wasted?"

3. In the historical US data shown, a buyer who held for ten years came out ahead of a renter for every start month that could be measured. That covers about 15 years of start months. The tiles at the end are unmeasured, not renter wins. The closing question suggests the video is about to look at whether rent is really wasted money.

4. The animation gives no direct advice. A viewer might infer that buying and holding for ten years has beaten renting in the past. The "not a forecast" label and the closing question argue against treating that as a rule. It also doesn't tell you whether buying is better for your own price, rate, rent or time horizon.

5. The animation itself suggested the historical result, through the lit tiles and the "every one (100%)" caption. It also suggested caution, through the "history, not a forecast" and "illustrative" labels. Any buy-versus-rent advice would be my own conclusion, because the frames give none.
